content: I want to build an app to save and manage bookmarks.

The draft specification is ready for review.

- Feature directory: [specs/001-manage-bookmarks](/work/specs/001-manage-bookmarks)
- Specification: [spec.md](/work/specs/001-manage-bookmarks/spec.md)
- Quality checklist: [requirements.md](/work/specs/001-manage-bookmarks/checklists/requirements.md)
- Validation: All 16 checks passed

The proposed first release covers saving, opening, editing, deleting, tagging, searching, filtering, and sorting bookmarks. It assumes a personal single-user app without accounts, sharing, browser extensions, imports, or automatic page metadata.

Please approve the specification or tell me what you’d like changed. I will not begin implementation planning until you approve it.

Thanks for putting this together — it's clear and easy to read. A few things jump out when I picture actually using it, so I'm not quite ready to approve.

The biggest one is saving. In your assumptions you've decided I'd type in the title myself every time. That's not what I want. When I paste in a link, I'd expect the app to go and fetch the page's title (and ideally its description and little site icon) for me automatically, so I usually don't have to type anything — and then I can tweak that title or description if I feel like it, before or after saving. Having to hand-type a title for every link is exactly the tedious part I'm hoping this app saves me from. Please fold that in.

On searching, what you have feels a bit thin for how I'd really use it. Two things I'd expect: I want to be able to search my tags specifically (not just stumble on them mixed into everything), and if I put something in quotes I'd expect it to find that exact phrase rather than the loose words. Down the line I'd also love to combine things — like "find me anything about Rome that's tagged either article or book" — so please make sure the search side is designed with that kind of combining in mind, not just a single plain keyword.

One more from the organizing side: I'd expect to be able to mark a link as "read this later" and then pull up just those unread ones on their own when I have time, and check them off once I've read them. That matters to me for keeping on top of things.

The duplicate handling you described — warning me and sending me to the existing bookmark instead of making a copy — is exactly right, so keep that.

Could you revise the spec with those changes and bring it back?

content:
The specification has been revised and revalidated.

Key additions:

- Automatic retrieval of page title, description, and site icon.
- Editable retrieved title and description before and after saving.
- Graceful fallback when metadata cannot be retrieved.
- Exact-phrase searches using quotation marks.
- Tag-specific search and multiple tag alternatives.
- Combined text, phrase, and tag conditions.
- Read-later collection with explicit read/unread status.
- Dedicated unread read-later view.
- Original duplicate-bookmark handling retained unchanged.

Updated artifacts:

- [Revised specification](/work/specs/001-manage-bookmarks/spec.md)
- [Quality checklist](/work/specs/001-manage-bookmarks/checklists/requirements.md)

All 16 quality checks pass. Planning remains paused pending your approval of the revised specification.

This looks great — you've captured everything I was worried about.

The saving flow is right: I paste a link, it fills in the title, description, and site icon for me, I can adjust them if I want, and if a page won't give up its details I can still save without getting stuck. The searching now does what I pictured — exact phrases in quotes, searching by tag, and combining something like "Rome" with either the article or book tag. And the read-later list with marking things read or unread is exactly the deliberate reading queue I had in mind. Good that the duplicate handling stayed the same.

I'm happy with the specification as written. You can go ahead and move on to planning.

The implementation plan is ready for review.

- [Implementation plan](/work/specs/001-manage-bookmarks/plan.md)

The plan uses one Node.js 24 application serving a React client and Fastify API, with SQLite persistence. Metadata retrieval receives a dedicated SSRF-hardened boundary, while search is parsed into an extensible expression model before database execution.

The OpenAPI file received structural validation; a full OpenAPI validator is not installed yet. No application code or task breakdown has been created.

Please approve the plan or identify any changes. Once approved, I’ll generate the dependency-ordered implementation tasks.

This all sounds sensible to me. I don't follow every technical detail, but what matters to me is that it lines up with what we agreed, and it does — saving from a pasted link with the page details filled in, catching duplicates, the search that lets me do exact phrases and combine a word like "Rome" with either the article or book tag, and the read-later queue. I like that fetching page details can't get in the way of just saving a link.

The plan looks good to me. Please go ahead and generate the implementation tasks.

The implementation task breakdown is ready:

- [tasks.md](/work/specs/001-manage-bookmarks/tasks.md)

Summary:

- 69 dependency-ordered tasks
- Setup: 5
- Foundation: 8
- Saving and metadata: 18
- Search and organization: 13
- Read-later queue: 9
- Editing and deletion: 8
- Final validation and polish: 8

All tasks passed format validation and include explicit file paths. Parallel opportunities and independent test criteria are documented for every user story.

The suggested MVP is User Story 1: paste a link, retrieve editable metadata safely, save despite retrieval failures, reopen it, and prevent duplicates. No application code has been implemented yet.

The task list covers all the parts we talked about, and starting with the save-and-reopen flow as the first milestone makes sense to me — that's the heart of it. Go ahead and start building. I'm looking forward to trying it out.

content:
The bookmark manager is built and ready to try at:

**http://maker:4000**

Implemented:

- Automatic title, description, and site-icon retrieval with fallback
- Duplicate detection
- Exact phrases, tag searches, and combined queries
- Tag filters and sorting
- Read-later and read/unread workflows
- Editing and confirmed deletion
- Persistent SQLite storage
- Responsive, keyboard-accessible interface

Validation passed:

- 28 unit/integration tests
- 2 Chromium end-to-end checks
- TypeScript, lint, and production build
- Automated accessibility scan
- 1,000-bookmark performance test
- Dependency audit with zero known vulnerabilities

Supporting files:

- [README](/work/README.md)
- [Validation report](/work/specs/001-manage-bookmarks/validation.md)
- [Completed tasks](/work/specs/001-manage-bookmarks/tasks.md)
- [Review screenshot](/work/prototypes/bookmark-manager.png)

I spent some time actually clicking around and trying it, and it does everything I was hoping for.

I pasted a link and it went and pulled the page's title for me, and when the page didn't offer a description or icon it just told me so and still let me save — exactly the "never gets in my way" behaviour I wanted. Saving the same address again warned me it was already there and pointed me to the one I'd already saved instead of making a copy. Search handled the fussy cases nicely: an exact phrase in quotes, searching by tag, and the combined "Example with either the article or book tag" query all returned the right thing, and a no-match search gave me a clean empty result. The read-later list showed only my unread items, and marking one as read dropped it off that list while keeping it in my library, with the option to flip it back. Editing and the confirm-before-delete both worked.

This is the bookmark app I asked for. I'm happy to accept it. Nicely done.

I do have a couple of ideas I might want later — things like keeping a saved copy of a page in case it disappears, and importing my existing browser bookmarks — but those are wishes for another round, not anything missing from what we agreed. Please just jot them down for the future; they don't hold up today's version.
